This article explores various aspects of specimen and sample handling in clinical diagnosis, including the importance of proper blood and urine collection, additives used in these samples, contamination risks, and special considerations for specific analytes.

exam: What is the first step you would take if a patient’s serum potassium is 6.5 mmol/L? — Check sample handling, look for haemolysis, repeat test if necessary.
Why should a blood culture be drawn before starting antibiotics? — To avoid false negatives caused by antibiotics killing organisms.
A patient with malaria has a low platelet count; how can you distinguish true thrombocytopenia from a pre‑analytical artefact? — Look for platelet clumping, check the smear, and repeat the count.
When is it acceptable to use a point‑of‑care glucose meter instead of laboratory glucose? — In emergencies where transport time is >30 minutes and the patient is unstable.
Why is a urine sample collected in a clean container important in diagnosing schistosomiasis? — To avoid contamination with soil or water that can give false positives.
If a patient’s CBC shows a low red cell count but the smear is normal, what is the likely cause? — Haemolysis during transport or improper anticoagulant use.
ai.title: Sample Handling in Clinical Diagnosis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Proper collection, transport and storage of specimens are essential for accurate results. In low‑resource settings, simple, cost‑effective practices can prevent pre‑analytical errors that mimic disease.

sections.p: Sample handling refers to all steps from patient preparation to laboratory receipt that can affect test accuracy. Errors here are called pre‑analytical errors and can lead to false positives or negatives.
Pre‑analytical errors are graded by their impact on patient care: minor (no clinical consequence), moderate (may alter management), major (could lead to misdiagnosis or harm).

Common causes in East African hospitals include inadequate venipuncture technique, delayed transport, incorrect anticoagulant use, and temperature excursions. Herbal remedies can also interfere with assays.

sections.p: Clinically, you may see unexpected lab values: low hemoglobin due to haemolysis, falsely low glucose from delayed transport, or elevated creatinine from dehydration.
The main investigations are the lab tests themselves, but you must ask why each test was ordered and whether the specimen was handled correctly.

t.b: Low RBC count indicates anemia; low platelets suggest thrombocytopenia. Hemolysis will falsely lower RBCs and raise potassium.
Low glucose may be true hypoglycaemia or due to delayed transport; high glucose indicates hyperglycaemia.
Elevated creatinine suggests renal impairment; dehydration can falsely raise it.
Proteinuria may be true or due to contamination; haematuria may be from infection or stone.
Positive culture confirms infection; contamination can give false positives.
